Williams's contribution came first, and only afterwards was Thomas Nagel's essay \"Moral Luck\" reprinted in his 1979 collection Mortal Questions. Two commitments organize the ensuing dispute. Because the control principle holds that agents are morally assessable only for what lies within their control, it gave rise to the category of resultant moral luck, which concerns the influence of uncontrolled outcomes on judgments of blame. The control principle is accepted without dissent by contemporary moral philosophers, an unqualified consensus that cannot be squared with the recognition that outcomes lying beyond an agent's control do shape judgments of blame; the two cannot both be true. The problem is not a recent invention. Book III of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics discusses voluntary action, ignorance, and culpability, anticipating by many centuries the modern treatment of culpable ignorance that came after it. That culpable ignorance accounts trace blame to an earlier failure to inquire into foreseeable risks is confirmed by Holly Smith's account, which distinguishes a benighting act from the later unwitting wrongful act. Restated in the idiom of law, that is precisely the principle by which negligence in tort law is assessed against a reasonable person standard of foreseeable risk; whereas quality of will accounts fix blame on the agent's motives, the tort standard sets motive aside and asks only what a reasonable person would have anticipated. Any such retrospective assessment, however, must reckon with a distortion in the assessors themselves. Hindsight bias leads evaluators to overestimate how predictable an outcome was before it occurred, and it is that inflation of predictability which made the harm foreseeable to a reasonably prudent agent at the time of the action. Adjudication therefore rests on a strict either/or: either the harm was foreseeable in just that way, or the harm was not foreseeable to a reasonably prudent agent at the time of the action, and exactly one of these must hold, never both at once.
